analysis.one_liner: Requires big multinational companies to publicly disclose profits, taxes, and subsidiaries country by country.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 8 senators backing it, was sent to the Senate Banking Committee on May 11, 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Multinational corporations can report low profits in high-tax countries and high profits in tax havens by moving money and ownership between their own subsidiaries. This bill would force companies above a revenue threshold to file an annual public report with the SEC showing, for every country where they operate: their subsidiaries, sales, profits, taxes paid, employees, and physical assets. That data would expose which companies book profits in places like the Cayman Islands while selling mostly in the US and Europe, giving regulators, investors, and the public the facts to push back on profit shifting.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently make up for the revenue corporations avoid by shifting profits offshore; small businesses that compete against multinationals with lower effective tax rates; investors and journalists who would get standardized, machine-readable country-by-country data; and tax authorities whose enforcement depends on exactly this kind of information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and small businesses competing with multinationals

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered issuers to file an annual SEC report showing, for each tax jurisdiction: revenues from and outside intercompany transactions, profit or loss before tax, income tax paid and accrued, stated capital, accumulated earnings, full-time-equivalent employees, and the net book value of tangible assets [S3].
The reports must also name every constituent entity, its tax jurisdiction of residence and incorporation, its tax ID, and its main business activities [S3].
The information must be filed in a machine-readable format and made available to the public online, so anyone — not just regulators — can analyze it [S3].
The bill directs the SEC to issue a proposed rule within 270 days and a final rule within one year of enactment, with the disclosure requirement taking effect one year after the final rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational companies, which would bear the cost of compiling and filing the reports and would lose the privacy that currently shields their country-by-country profit and tax positions from scrutiny; tax haven jurisdictions and offshore financial services providers, whose business model depends on secrecy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinational corporations and tax haven jurisdictions

drawbacks.text: The reporting itself raises no money. It creates transparency that only improves tax collection if regulators and lawmakers then act on it; a disclosure mandate is a first step, not enforcement [S3].

Multinational companies would face new compliance costs to assemble subsidiary-level data across dozens of jurisdictions each year, and the bill would require public disclosure of profits and taxes by country, which some companies view as commercially sensitive [S3].

Because the bill counts any territory or possession of the United States with fiscal autonomy as a tax jurisdiction, it would put US territories' tax arrangements under the same public spotlight as foreign havens, which territories could fairly object to [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large but indirect: country-by-country reporting is the standard tool tax authorities and researchers use to detect profit shifting, which costs the US tens of billions of dollars a year in avoided corporate tax. The costs are real but comparatively small — compliance expenses for large companies and the end of secrecy around where multinationals book profits. The main design limitation is that disclosure alone does not collect a dollar of tax; it equips the people who could.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced the bill on May 11, 2021, joined by Sens. Klobuchar, Duckworth, Whitehouse, Sanders, Durbin, Blumenthal, and Smith [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].

The CRS summary describes a matching disclosure requirement: certain issuers of securities must annually disclose the tax jurisdiction, income, and assets of their constituent entities on a country-by-country basis [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinationals that shift profits offshore kept the status quo: no public country-by-country data, and no SEC rulemaking. The committee that declined to act avoided a fight with corporate interests over disclosure.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its name and framing: forcing disclosure of tax havens and offshoring

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and independents
for.role: Original cosponsors (Klobuchar, Duckworth, Whitehouse, Sanders, Durbin, Blumenthal, Smith)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it stayed at referral for the remaining 20 months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run Banking Committee did not advance it.

industries.note: The bill would end the secrecy that lets multinationals book profits in low-tax jurisdictions while doing business elsewhere, exposing effective tax rates country by country. The public cost of that profit shifting is borne by ordinary taxpayers, so the industry's interest here runs against theirs.

industries.industry: Offshore financial centers and tax haven jurisdictions
industries.note: Secrecy about where companies book profits is central to the haven business model; public country-by-country data would make it much harder to sell. The bill explicitly counts non-country jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy as reportable tax jurisdictions.
